spark.summary: Caching keeps a reusable copy of data so an application can avoid repeating a database query, calculation, or network call. It can make responses faster and reduce database load. The trade-off: the copy may be out of date.
spark.keyTakeaway: Keep a clear source of truth. Decide how stale a cached value may be, how to refresh it, and what happens when the cache is empty or unavailable.

concept.whyItMatters: Many requests ask for the same information. Reusing a cached result leaves the database more capacity for other work. A 10x traffic surge without a robust caching layer causes database saturation. The benefit depends on how often requests reuse data and how much work a hit avoids.

whenNotToUse: Values that change so often that cached copies are rarely reused.

examples.title: A product description
examples.scenario: GET /products/42 checks Redis for product:42. On a miss, the application reads PostgreSQL and caches the description for about five minutes.
examples.outcome: Later requests reuse the description without reading PostgreSQL. A product edit updates the database and invalidates the cached copy.

examples.title: A popular homepage
examples.scenario: Many requests need the same homepage response. One worker refreshes the cached response while other requests wait briefly or use an explicitly allowed stale copy.
examples.outcome: Concurrent requests avoid rebuilding the same response independently. Stale serving needs a defined maximum age and must not be used where outdated data is unacceptable.

tradeOffs.pro: A local cache avoids network calls.
tradeOffs.con: Each application instance has its own copy. A shared cache reduces duplication but adds a network dependency.

tradeOffs.pro: TTL is simple; invalidation can remove outdated data sooner.
tradeOffs.con: Expiry permits stale reads, and invalidation can fail or race with a concurrent refill. Neither alone guarantees instant freshness.

tradeOffs.pro: More capacity can retain a larger reusable working set.
tradeOffs.con: Extra memory costs money and may not help when requests rarely reuse data. Cold starts still need controlled refilling.

failureModes.name: Many keys expire together
failureModes.description: A burst of misses sends extra traffic to the database. This is called a cache avalanche.
failureModes.mitigation: Add random TTL jitter and stagger refilling. Limit database concurrency as a safety net.

failureModes.name: One popular key expires
failureModes.description: Many requests try to rebuild the same value at once. This is a cache stampede, also called hot-key breakdown.
failureModes.mitigation: Coalesce refreshes so one worker loads the value. Other requests wait for a bounded time or use an explicitly allowed stale copy.

failureModes.name: Requests target missing records
failureModes.description: Repeated requests for nonexistent IDs keep reaching the database. This is cache penetration.
failureModes.mitigation: Validate inputs, briefly cache not-found results, and rate-limit abuse. A Bloom filter is safe to reject records only when it accurately represents the current dataset.

failureModes.name: The cache is unavailable
failureModes.description: Unrestricted fallback can overwhelm the database.
failureModes.mitigation: Use short cache timeouts, bounded fallback, circuit breakers, and load shedding. Sometimes an error is safer than another database query.

failureModes.name: An old value refills the cache
failureModes.description: A reader fetches an old database value, a writer updates the database and invalidates the key, then the reader caches the old value.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a coordinated, version-aware protocol when stronger freshness is needed. Short TTLs reduce exposure but do not eliminate this race.

commonMistakes: Treating an expendable cache as durable storage.
Leaving memory limits, connections, timeouts, or retries unbounded.
Omitting tenant, user, locale, or other response-changing inputs from cache keys.
Assuming write-through automatically provides strong consistency.
Measuring only hit rate instead of response latency, cache errors, evictions, and database load.

sections.content:
## Do the work once. Reuse the result.

**Caching** allows systems to do the work once and reuse the result. Many requests ask for the same information. Reusing a cached result leaves the database more capacity for other work. The benefit depends on how often requests reuse data and how much work a hit avoids.

- Cache hit: the requested value is found and can be reused.
- Cache miss: the application fetches or computes the value.
- TTL (time to live): how long an entry may remain before it expires. It can still become stale before expiry.
- Invalidation: removing a cached copy when its source changes.
- Eviction: removing entries to stay within a memory limit, sometimes before their TTL expires.

### Good candidates

- Frequently read product descriptions or reference data.
- Expensive reports that can tolerate a short delay in freshness.
- Public content and static assets served through a CDN.

### Think twice

- Values that change so often that cached copies are rarely reused.
- Correctness-critical decisions based only on potentially stale balances, prices, or stock counts.
- Already-cheap queries where caching adds little measurable benefit.

## A request, step by step

This cache-aside example uses Redis for a reusable copy and PostgreSQL as the source of truth. The application queries the database and fills the cache; Redis does not query PostgreSQL itself.

`GET /products/42` checks Redis for `product:42`. On a miss, the application reads PostgreSQL and caches the description for about five minutes.

sections.content:
## Keeping data fresh

After a product edit, commit the database update, then delete `product:42` from Redis. The next miss loads a fresh copy.

This is not atomic across both systems. Invalidation can fail. A reader can also fetch an old value before the update and refill it after invalidation. Short TTLs limit exposure but do not eliminate that race. Stronger freshness needs a coordinated, version-aware protocol.

For a correctness-critical transaction, validate the decision in the authoritative system rather than relying only on a stale cached value.

## Data movement is not a consistency guarantee

| Pattern | How it works | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Cache-aside | Application loads missing data and fills the cache. | Misses are slower; invalidation and refill can race. |
| Write-through | A caching layer synchronously persists writes to the database. | Adds write latency; partial failures and concurrency still need coordination. |
| Write-behind | Writes are persisted to the database later. | Unpersisted acknowledged updates can be lost without durable recovery. |
| Refresh-ahead | Refresh hot entries before expiry. | Adds background work and does not guarantee fresh data. |

## Protect the database on a bad day.

### Many keys expire together

A burst of misses sends extra traffic to the database. This is called a cache avalanche.

Add random TTL jitter and stagger refilling. Limit database concurrency as a safety net.

### One popular key expires

Many requests try to rebuild the same value at once. This is a cache stampede, also called hot-key breakdown.

Coalesce refreshes so one worker loads the value. Other requests wait for a bounded time or use an explicitly allowed stale copy.

### Requests target missing records

Repeated requests for nonexistent IDs keep reaching the database. This is cache penetration.

Validate inputs, briefly cache not-found results, and rate-limit abuse. A Bloom filter is safe to reject records only when it accurately represents the current dataset.

### The cache is unavailable

Unrestricted fallback can overwhelm the database.

Use short cache timeouts, bounded fallback, circuit breakers, and load shedding. Sometimes an error is safer than another database query.

### An old value refills the cache

A reader fetches an old database value, a writer updates the database and invalidates the key, then the reader caches the old value.

Use a coordinated, version-aware protocol when stronger freshness is needed. Short TTLs reduce exposure but do not eliminate this race.

## Expiry without a traffic spike

Use `TTL = base TTL + random offset`. With a base of 300 seconds and an offset between -30 and +30 seconds, entries expire after 270–330 seconds. An offset of +14 gives 314 seconds.

Jitter spreads expiry across different keys. It does not protect a single hot key; use refresh coalescing for that.

If refresh coordination uses a distributed lock, use an expiring lease, a unique owner token, and atomic owner-checked release. Bound waiting and retries, and handle work that outlasts the lease.

## Start small and measure

Begin with one cache layer. Set a memory budget and eviction policy. Bound client connections, timeouts, and database fallback.

Measure hit rate alongside end-to-end latency, cache errors, evictions, refresh duration, and database load. Add local caches or CDN layers only when the workload justifies their extra invalidation rules and failure modes.

questions.title: In-Memory Cache Latency Advantage
questions.prompt: Why does an in-memory key-value cache (e.g. Redis, Memcached) serve read requests orders of magnitude faster than a traditional relational database?

options.text: It stores data on local NVMe solid-state storage without operating system page caches.
options.explanation: In-memory caches operate in RAM rather than relying on disk storage.

options.text: It keeps data structures resident in volatile RAM and uses O(1) hash table lookups, eliminating disk I/O, B-tree traversals, and relational join locks.
options.explanation: Correct! RAM access latency (~100ns) and in-memory hash tables bypass slow disk I/O and query planning overhead.

rubric.excellent: Identifies direct RAM access, elimination of disk I/O seek overhead, and O(1) in-memory index structures.
rubric.acceptable: Mentions that reading from memory is faster than disk.
rubric.gap: Confuses RAM storage with disk or network caching.

questions.sampleSolution: In-memory caches store data directly in RAM with O(1) hash tables, avoiding disk I/O and query execution planning.
questions.explanation: RAM access operates at nanosecond scale, whereas disk seeks and complex relational query evaluation require milliseconds.

interviewProblems.title: High-Concurrency Flash Sale Seat Locking
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are designing the ticketing platform for a concert drop with 100,000 concurrent users. How do you prevent double-booking seats while protecting PostgreSQL from crashing?
constraints: Max seat lock duration is 10 minutes.

dimensions.name: Read/Write Decoupling
dimensions.description: Serving seat map reads from CDN/Redis.

dimensions.name: Atomic Locking Mechanics
dimensions.description: Using SETNX for atomic lock acquiring.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Decouple seat map reads to Redis. Acquire atomic seat lock using SETNX key user_id NX PX 600000. Process payment asynchronously via Kafka.
commonPitfalls: Querying PostgreSQL directly for seat availability during a drop.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Caching keeps a reusable copy of data so an application can avoid repeating a database query, calculation, or network call. It can make responses faster and reduce database load. The trade-off: the copy may be out of date.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Redis applies the primary invariant and coordinates with PostgreSQL.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, PostgreSQL experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Add random TTL jitter and stagger refilling. Limit database concurrency as a safety net.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Keep a clear source of truth. Decide how stale a cached value may be, how to refresh it, and what happens when the cache is empty or unavailable.
Avoid trap: Treating an expendable cache as durable storage.
Avoid trap: Leaving memory limits, connections, timeouts, or retries unbounded.
When to reach for it: Frequently read product descriptions or reference data.

steps: Establish baseline invariants for Caching before scaling.

putItTogether.outcome: Later requests reuse the description without reading PostgreSQL. A product edit updates the database and invalidates the cached copy.
